This game has absolutely fantastic potential and I am overall really glad it released in EA rather than claiming to be a final product. The game has small issues but runs well on low settings (which is ideal for me as my hardware is lacking) and has brilliant use of sound and visual effects to keep you on your toes at all times. 
The crafting system is similar to other games and represents a challenge but also a progression aspect to work through as you play, I played a lot of the beta release and can see the changes already made based on the feedback received which is reassuring from a gaming company that they are listening to their player base!
Overall it's a cinematic, immersive experience where you really have to consider not only the physical health of your character but also the mental affect your environment is having on you as you traverse it's dangers. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for an escape to the wild in the comfort of your own home, there's a lot more to come for this game and I really do believe it will live up to it's slightly larger opening price tag in the coming releases - I will definitely be playing more and I hope to see a coop aspect added in the future so I can survive with friends too!

This is a survival game that you can tell the developers care about. The game definitely didn't launch perfect, but they are updating this game nonstop and have come a long way. The visuals in this game are top-tier, and for the most part is decently optimized except around a few assets.   The music in the game is also phenomenal, it actually makes you feel hopeless and dreadful, which is exactly what it should be doing when the player is stuck in a snowy forest trying everything they can to survive. Combat has gotten an overhaul and feels WAY better, AI has improved although could still use some improvement, and the devs have been adding lots of extra content such as a new gamemode and a continuation of the extremely short story on launch. The game is not multiplayer however I feel it that is a good choice to build on atmosphere and horror. I would still love to see it though.

Winter Survival by Drago Entertainment emerges as a compelling addition to the survival genre on Steam, plunging players into a harsh, snow-covered wilderness where survival is a constant battle against the elements, wildlife, and one's own sanity:

Pros:
- Rich Survival Gameplay: Features an intricate blend of combat, stealth, base building, and a unique sanity system, ensuring a multifaceted survival experience​​​​​​.
-Authentic Survival Experience: The game places a heavy emphasis on realism, requiring players to manage body temperature, hunger, thirst, and mental health while contending with environmental hazards and predatory wildlife​​.
- Multiple Game Modes: With story mode, Coldwave, and Endless modes, it caters to a wide range of player preferences, offering both narrative-driven exploration and sandbox survival challenges​

Cons: 
- Early Access Limitations: Currently in Early Access, players may encounter bugs and incomplete features, with the game’s full potential still to be realized through community feedback and further development​​.
- Steep Learning Curve: Newcomers might find the game’s survival mechanics daunting, requiring careful management of resources and strategic planning from the start​​.
- Complex Sanity and Trauma System: The inclusion of a sanity and trauma system adds depth but also complexity, with the potential for permanent debuffs that can significantly impact gameplay and frustrate unprepared players and feels not quite properly balanced

Winter Survival earns a frosty yet fiery rating of 4/5, marking it as a beacon for those seeking a survival game with depth and realism. It's a testament to the enduring appeal of the genre, inviting players to brave its icy world.

Hi there – first off, thanks for creating such an atmospheric and promising survival experience. I’d love to share a few ideas and questions regarding future weather and snow mechanics:

Are there plans to implement dynamic weather events like blizzards or storms that significantly affect the player, environment, and buildings?

And are you considering varying snow levels or types – for example:
- standard snow cover,
- deep snow that slows movement,
- avalanches that could be triggered and cause damage or death?

It would be amazing to have situations where you spot a snowstorm approaching and are forced to take shelter, barricade yourself inside, and survive the night near a fire, with the storm raging outside.

The next morning, your door might be snowed in, and you'd need to dig your way out.
Of course, this would require a solid snow physics system, one that plausibly affects terrain, movement, structures, and visibility – but it could truly elevate the game’s immersion and uniqueness.

Is something like this on your roadmap?

Thanks for reading – looking forward to what’s next!

To compare a video game to real life, is not a good comparison, because in the wild the animals in this game would likely run away from you before you got close. Unless you spook a grizzle and they charge as a fear response, or it has cubs; nine times out of ten that animal will be gone before you knew it was there, and I know people that keep wolves as pets. So a hyper-realistic game would be you alone in the cold, rarely seeing an animal, and that is boring. I compare this to Long Dark and I think this game has the potential to be a better, game; with things such as base building, no locking perks in customization mode, and no cabin fever. Better encounters with animals, not RNG mose spamming, Not having ones save deleted on death, I don't like permadeath. It is early access and does have bugs, but for a video game, I enjoy it.

Just about anything you can find should be of some use, so looting is very important. Well, in this weather, crafting warmer clothes should be on top of the list.

Graphics are really nice, great textures, effects and awesome skyboxes. I just love to stand outside while the grass is swaying in the cold wind while getting hypothermia.

I tested the game on i5-12400F, RX 6800 XT 16GB, 32GB DDR5 RAM and m.2 SSD. On 1080p I get around 50 to 60 fps with epic settings, while jumping up to 1440p takes at least 25 fps away. It apparently has FSR but it can't be enabled. Optimization is very much needed.

I'm a big survival fan, I play all open world crafting survival games. This one is amongst the best in my opinion. I payed for a copy along with my wife because steam family sharing was not working for the game yesterday, so we had to buy it twice. But oh well. I have not yet explored the whole game. I'm just so saddened by all the MIXED reviews. I don't understand why. The game is not 100%. But it's still amazing and fun. We use Xbox controllers, and it feels like there could be some work done with the menus. The movement dragging clicking for controllers still feels off. Like the game wants you to use a keyboard. But no big deal still workable. One thing I don't like is how the charge-up on the spear goes away after 5 seconds. You have to be really close to the wolf to start the charge up. But I've had no problem killing them. There's so much to craft, to learn, to find. Resources seem easy to find, which is awesome. Wish the wood would keep the fire going longer though. Anyways I don't want to make this too long. But I speak for myself and my wife and we both recommend this game to anyone who likes survival games. She will also be posting her review once she's ready, but I'm sure hers will be thumbs up as well. Don't pay attention to the mixed part yall, this game is way better than that. The development team seems to truly care about this project and we look forward to everything to come.

This is a game I've been waiting for since the first demo version and am excited to see the vision coming together with the Early Access Release. 
I love the concept, and the developers have put a lot of time and effort into crafting an immersive and bleakly picturesque world to die or go crazy in. 

The Good
After several delays to the early access launch date I think the developers have found a good balance between rounding out the rough edges of the demo releases and leaving room for the game to grow. 

The graphics are smooth and the many dynamic elements like moving auroras and vanishing hallucinations put the video card to work (NVidia RSTX 3080) but without any issues. I haven't experienced any crashing or freezing and have managed to avoid getting stuck anywhere thus far. 

The survival dynamics of the game make you "work for it" to keep playing. I enjoy that it makes the survival aspect more engaging, but unlike games like Stranded Deep and The Forest where you can have a base built and running your first day I've found it takes closer to a week of game time to progress far enough to get to that point. 

The best parts of the game though are the little surprises (both good and bad) that come from the layers-deep sanity and buff/debuff system. Turn off your flashlight and you're afraid of the dark, bring it back on or light a torch and you feel better. Walk through a creek and your boots get wet, slowing your movement and increasing your heat loss until you dry them out. Eat snow and gain water but lose body heat. And my personal favorite, make it a few days and run away from enough wolves in a row without learning about the bathing mechanic and you gain a "stench" factor that makes you attractable to animals more easily. 

Lastly, I'll just comment that I enjoy the encumbrance / weight system that mimics the Bethesda Fallout / Starfield model. It works a lot better than the restrictive limited carry slots of other recent open world survival craft games. 

It's hard, the hardest learning curve I've had since They Are Billions (yes different genre but iykyk), but engaging and you really feel like you earn those restful moments back at the cabin where you can finally 

The Bad
The game, despite the learning curve, keeps you within the playable tutorial. I'm around 4 hours in and only just able to start building and adding to a base. In the demos you could start patching up your hut and making it "liveable" in an hour or two and that felt better balanced. I get that the game is trying to let you feel out all the different survival and sanity mechanics, but give me a hammer so I can start patching holes in my woodcutter's cottage and keeping the heat in already!

The game also seems to mock you at times. I've found multiple spears looking pointy and tantilizingly effective at taking down those ever-present wolves or even a stag for some meat, but alas - I haven't found the uncraftable spear HOLDER yet, so I can't even pick one up at the expense of holding onto other equipment. 

The game is HARD, and you don't get much reward for the effort you put into things. Nearly find one of your friends after sneaking through a cave full of sleeping wolves and you get rewarded with an overencumbrance of items you largely can't craft with yet at this stage of the game and a half game-day hike back to your base to start another quest. Still, the narrative moves things along and at least it's clear "what comes next".

Hello, MF Kraven here & today I'm gonna be doing a First Impressions on the upcoming early access Winter Survival. When I do 1st impressions, I like talking about the game, my experience and give a wishlist at the end. At it's core it's an open world survival, exploration/hunting game. It's heavily reliant on stealth as not only will the cold be out to get ya, but predators as well. You play as Danny, a man struggling with his mental health- in the wilderness of a frigid Washington State Park. Being as I've spent the last couple of years in Montana- I can completely attest that being outside in that kind of weather sucks. But anyways, the reason I'm doing a first impressions & not a review is because I really liked this game full disclosure BUT there is a LOT of work & quality of life improvements Winter Survival desperately needs.

 
I'll start with the main menus & what made me make the decision of showing mercy. There are three game modes, Story. Endless. & Cold Wave. I only dove into Story & Endless as Cold Wave is coming soon. There are two difficulty settings, Explorer (easy) & Survivalist (hard). Story mode isn't complete, only prologue & first chapter are available & it takes you through HOW Danny & his friends got there, and the dangers that presented your party. Without giving too much away, Danny probably needs to seek some sort of help... Where I think Winter Survival has thee most potential however is the Endless Mode. So you get taken to a menu where you can choose your story, how you got where you are and then spawn with good or less than desirable conditions. I dipped my feet into two different scenarios & both times made me feel like I was getting a completely different adventure. A+ for that!!!

In all scenarios you're tasked with building shelter for yourself, while leveling up. At first I didn't really take notice of the leveling system as stuff would just automatically unlock after leveling up, but once i visited the Adaptations menu i saw what skills & builds I actually got. The building mechanic need work in my opinion as everything is just really hard to make, it'll have you running around in circles & if you plan on using a hammer to deconstruct buildings nearby which you can, it has about 10 uses before you need to build another one. And now material is plentiful but sometimes I had trouble looking for certain things like big branches on the floor so I was thankful for X RAY VISION. I normally don't like it in games, but with the struggling mental health & all that- I thought I could give it a pass. So to touch on that, there's a sanity system that makes your survival much harder the more you play it. You'll get de-buffed with things like seeing animals that aren't there, getting blurry vision among other ailments. As far as I see, there isn't a way to cure any of the ailments but you can slow the deterioration of your mind by- well, taking care of yourself. 

Hunting in game can be fun & real frustrating, as long as you track deer or rabbits certain movement you can kinda figure where to place snare traps and poke em with spears. WOLVES, boars and bears on the other hand are completely different beasts- obviously but you need to be on the defensive with a spear and if you're on easy just holding the spear will make your guy auto impale while in hard- you must time it just right. I had a pretty bad encounter where I couldn't equip my spear or pull up the inventory or do much of anything but run really that is really gonna ruin my current save as my mental health went down the drain HARD for that interaction. 

Then when building my shelter I had already built a fire and the only way to destroy the fire was to destroy the foundation that I built it on BUT when I did that, the two side walls, and roofing had to be rebuilt too & of course i had to gather ALL the material to rebuild it

The game is beautiful though, and opening up my window as I play this with minimal clothing (it's 2 degrees and snowing currently where i live) really immersed me into Winter Survival. 

My Wishlist for Winter Survival

-Completely change the fighting mechanic, I couldn't make a spear- had to find one and even when I tried using it, I couldn't. Not being able to use my axe or any other weapon to attack made me lose my immersion
-tweaks to the sanity system on endless mode. maybe having tea can help soothe Danny's mind or beating a wolf can give you a buff that can restore one of the six symptoms for a day or two?
-stuff should cost maybe half of what it does to craft, i keep having to go back and forth and look for branches everywhere. it was cute at first but I just want to build (at least just in easy mode)
-more stuff to craft at lower levels. While food is readily available, even on easy the meter would run down fast and instead of eating berry after berry maybe cooking like 10 of em for some roasted berries? idk
-Save files to be more organized, I had 3 different saves going on and I didn't know what was what.
-MULTIPLAYER Mode! While it does defeat the purpose of the sanity system- i think it would be an awesome edition.

Pros:
The game is beautiful.  The music is haunting.  The sanity factor was a big draw for me.  

Cons: 
Limited destructability: Many things in the world should be salvageable with a good axe or knife, but are in fact uninteractable. 

Sanity and tiredness progress extremely rapidly, and there's no way to mitigate them in the early game:
      ~You don't get to keep your sleeping bag from the intro in story mode, and you don't learn to make a simple straw nest mat until much later.  You will faint and either freeze to death or get eaten very easily in the beginning for no good reason.

Food Spoilage is way too fast:
     ~The world is a refrigerator during the day and a freezer at night.  Meat shouldn't spoil so quickly, especially when cooked, if it's stored outside.  Berries should last for several days, indefinitely outside.  Aside from animals stealing your food, you shouldn't lose food to spoilage so quickly when you can just put them in a box outside. 
     ~There's no mechanism (that I know of so far) to dry or smoke meat to make it last longer. 

Knives are way too limited:
     ~There's no reason a flint knife can't be used to skin animals.  You don't get access to skinning until you can craft a bone knife (?!). 
     ~Also, knives should be usable for basic defense.  

Animal Fat is nearly useless:
    ~This shouldn't be the case.  Anyone who's watched any survival show or knows anything about bushcraft knows the saying: "Fat is Gold." Animal Fat needs to be far more useful than it is.  If nothing else, you should be able to fry it up in a frying pan and eat it.  But it should also be added to soups and stews to increase their buffs.  It should be usable to, when combined with dried or smoked meat, make Pemmican: basically our ancestors' long term food storage energy bar. It should be usable to waterproof leather to increase it's water resistance.  It should be more useful overall. 

Animal AI is strange:
     ~I see wolves eating deer kills, but when deer or rabbits are alive and near wolves, they completely ignore each other.  

Can't craft bow and arrows, but can craft a gun??
     ~This is just nonsensical.  There needs to be more ranged options than firearms and thrown rocks.  What's the point of finding catgut, for example, if I can't use it to make a bow?

More traps, please:
      ~With a shovel, an axe, and a knife, I should be able to make pit traps and spiked pit traps.  With rope, I should be able to make snares and drop traps.  There needs to be more options with this. 

Controller doesn't quite work yet:
     ~Controllers are usable, but they don't always work.  Pretty buggy, and requires using both Controller and MK to get by.  

All this being said, I do enjoy this game very much, and would like to see it improve. But right now it's just too limited to recommend.

From the first moments of the intro video, this game captured my intrigue. Pretty good intro, worth watching and gives some insight on what to expect. “Getting owned by nature” would be a fitting title for most survival games. You most likely know most of what to expect as you are probably a fan of the genre. Chopping, hauling, building, and riding the struggle bus…there is more to this one than just the basics of survival. Some room for improvement and some genre changing innovation, overall a pretty good mix that I am struggling to put down. While it doesnt have Valheim levels of building customization, or deep resource mining/crafting…this is a title that rewards exploration and facilitates self-determination more than alot of other survival games. Green Hell used to hold my top favorite survival slot, and I think it just got dethroned.

First lets get into the room for improvement, I am so fond of this game that burying this content farther down would be a disservice to readers. Mechanically speaking, this game has some troubles with scripted events. Outside of that I have had one problem that the devs confirmed was functioning as intended (must remove walls to upgrade floor, removing walls means removing roof, upgrading floor first will remove walls and roof). The story (and cold wave mode) rely kind of heavily on events that occur as a result of player action and unfortunately, in the first couple weeks of release there have been some problems on this front. The devs have been more responsive than most, and are steadily fixing the issues as far as I can tell. Should be a patch out in a couple days afaik. At worst these issues have cost me about 3-10 minutes of time to replay, and I finished the story well before all of them were addressed. Not a huge deal but non-zero none the less. In cold wave mode, some of these crashes have cost me entire runs. I don't love that but the devs indicated that it will be fixed shortly.

Regarding the gameplay, I think there is a purity to art that doesn’t shove its meaning directly in your face, allowing you to form your own conclusions that inevitably align with the artist’s vision. I felt this game was one of those cases. The earliest parts of the tutorial gave me some max payne / alan wake vibes, feeling that for sure. My first minute was staring at the pause screen at the beginning and thinking “how do I unfornicate this? Need food, shelter, and water, all the water and food wont help me if I freeze to death. Go.” The landscape looked lush and well populated, the animals strangely believable which was refreshing. I couldn’t get close to them except for the wolf who shot a ‘wolf missile’ at me. The only thing I felt was disbelief as my guy died. The whole intro section is well crafted, doesn’t club you over the head, and goes through nearly every mechanic you will need to understand…except for impale. Somehow I made it to the last fight in the story before I understood the impale mechanic, which made fighting wolves so much easier.

In one of the later acts the devs introduce a feature that I have never seen in a survival game before and I think its absolutely glorious. I would play a whole game centered around just this concept. Ive played every survival game that I have come across because I love the struggle (if you dont see one you loved in my library, drop a comment and point me at it =D). Nobody has covered [spoiler] being responsible for the survival of another person [/spoiler] and it is pretty well done, maybe [spoiler] they could have been more vulnerable to temperature [/spoiler] but it was thrilling and I was so locked in for this part of the game. Story wrapped up well and theres room in the plot for more developments. Loved the ride for sure.

Cold wave is a themed endless mode and oh my god I am so here for that. I have hardly been able to put this down. The devs look to run competitions periodically in ranked “slug it out with nature” mode and I have put up good scores both playing the objective as well as fighting out an epic turtle against the weather (cycle 74 &%^$ yeah!). No saves, except an exit/entry save if you have to quit mid run. I have been playing these in one sitting 1-2h straight through and it is amazing. Pure adrenaline and focus, every decision is mission critical. The intensity is so high in this game mode there is nothing that hasn’t been nerfed or patched out from other survival games that comes close. It’s like shooting up cortisol, not sure why anyone would do that but I f&cking love it.

The weather is nasty, the resources are scarce, the wildlife isn’t on your team, and at times it seems like the ground itself curses my name. The survival experience was so frantic I felt like I was chasing my tail just to stay vertical, which is about as real as it gets. You need to be able to identify when what you are doing isn’t working or you are going back to the load screen! Brutal, visceral melee vs a tenacious climate in a land that doesn’t want you there. Literally here for exactly that. Less than a month since release and I have hit 100+ hours? Insane. Waiting on this week's patch or I wouldn't have even had time to write this XD

Winter Survival, developed by DRAGO Entertainment and co-published by HeartBeat Games, is a harsh, slow-burning survival experience built around the brutality of winter wilderness and the fragility of the human mind. Instead of relying solely on the usual meters—hunger, warmth, stamina, and thirst—it tries to convey the emotional weight of isolation, fear, and trauma. You step into the role of Danny, an inexperienced outdoorsman who becomes stranded in an unforgiving frozen landscape after a disastrous expedition. From the opening moments, the game reinforces that you’re not a rugged survival icon—you’re overwhelmed, freezing, and profoundly alone. The journey becomes less about mastery and more about desperation, with every small achievement, from lighting a fire to locating shelter, feeling monumental.

Core survival systems drive the moment-to-moment gameplay. You must scavenge wood, craft basic tools, skin animals, purify water, and patch clothing just to keep the cold from killing you. The world doesn’t exist to support you—it actively resists you. Snowstorms reduce visibility and steal body heat, wolves track your scent, and wandering too long drains your energy faster than expected. Managing limited resources becomes a tense balancing act: warm yourself near a fire and risk drawing predators, or push deeper into the wilderness and gamble with frostbite or exhaustion. The crafting system encourages incremental progress rather than rapid advancement, giving you a constant sense of scraping by rather than flourishing. Exploration rewards curiosity, but it also punishes impatience, so every new step into the unknown carries layered risk.

What sets Winter Survival apart from many genre counterparts is its emphasis on psychological strain. Danny doesn’t simply get tired or hungry—he spirals. Hallucinations distort reality, imaginary sounds provoke panic, shadows look like stalking beasts, and moments of internal narration reveal a deteriorating mental state. These sequences blur the line between danger and paranoia, creating tension without relying solely on combat encounters. Sanity becomes as important as warmth or calories, influencing how players navigate the environment. It turns the wilderness into a metaphorical adversary, suggesting that surviving the cold may be easier than surviving yourself. While not always perfectly balanced or seamlessly integrated, it adds personality and thematic weight to the experience.

The game offers multiple modes that cater to different playstyles. Story Mode provides structure, character motivation, and emotional stakes, guiding new players through the mechanics and environment. Survival Mode strips away narrative and allows players to carve their own path—whether building a long-term base, mapping every region, or testing how long they can endure. Cold Wave Mode shifts into challenge territory, pitting players against increasingly hostile weather conditions in a more score-driven loop. Together, the modes help prevent monotony and extend replayability, even if the broader systems do not dramatically transform between them.

Visually, Winter Survival leans heavily into natural beauty and environmental dread. Snow-blown forests feel both serene and threatening, abandoned cabins communicate quiet tragedy, and distant animal silhouettes elicit a mix of curiosity and panic. The soundscape strengthens immersion—cracking ice, howling wind, quiet footsteps in deep snow, and sudden growls make every silence suspenseful. While character animations and UI elements occasionally lack refinement, the environmental presentation successfully evokes the loneliness and scale of the landscape. The world doesn’t feel empty by accident—it feels empty the way uninhabited wilderness should.

Despite its strengths, the game isn’t without rough edges. The onboarding process can feel overwhelming for newcomers, especially given how punishing the cold and wildlife can be early on. Systems aren’t always communicated clearly, leading to avoidable deaths and frustration. Performance optimization varies depending on hardware, and the demanding visuals and environmental effects may challenge lower-spec machines. Certain mechanics—particularly sanity effects—sometimes feel more like interruptions than meaningful gameplay consequences. Inventory management and crafting navigation can also become tedious over longer sessions, especially during repeat runs. These issues don’t ruin the experience, but they reveal its still-evolving nature.

For players who enjoy methodical, atmospheric survival experiences, Winter Survival delivers a compelling mixture of beauty and brutality. It rewards patience, observation, and restraint more than aggression or efficiency. Those expecting fast progression, streamlined crafting, or constant action may find it too slow or punishing, but players who appreciate tension, isolation, and environmental storytelling will likely connect with its intentions. It is a game best approached as a psychological endurance test rather than a power fantasy.

In the end, Winter Survival succeeds not by innovating every survival mechanic, but by grounding the genre in vulnerability—emotional, physical, and mental. It captures the terror of freezing wind, the relief of shelter, and the uneasy quiet that comes from knowing no one is coming to help. It’s imperfect, occasionally uneven, and at times frustrating, but it’s also immersive, atmospheric, and memorable. For players seeking a winter survival experience that values mood and struggle over spectacle, it’s a journey worth taking—if you’re willing to brave the cold.

Originally named, Winter Survival Simulator, I had the ability to play it many years before it's release and even a year before it's publicly released demo (content creators were given an early access beta build about a year before the demo / prologue released).

In my personal experience, I thoroughly enjoyed the beta version of the game and had even played all of the available content numerous times, having racked up more than 40 hours (yeah I dunno how.. it was just that good).

As a big fan of simulator and crafting type games, I was stoked for it's official release. I waited nearly 4 years since I played the early beta build and have left feedback to the publishers/devs long ago and even expressed my strong interest in the full release.

Well.. here we are today. I purchased the game (didn't get a free copy for the invaluable feedback + being an early beta tester, not that it really matters but wanted to share that with people so they knew this review was genuine) and I have to say that I'm unfortunately upset with what all was delivered.

The game being released in EA is fine and all but with it only having one act after nearly 4 years of development time from when I last played the beta build, this is what's most disheartening because I was truly expecting.. or at least hoping... for a full story game. 1 act after years of development is concerning for me and probably many others.

If the game released in EA with 2-3 acts and only about 3 acts left, then that would be understandable but in it's current state, it feels more like an extension of the demo / prologue build.

Now that I've shared a few of my personal thoughts on the game, let's get into brass tax and talk about the actual pros and cons or positives and negatives.

[b]Positives:[/b]
-Shared Craft Items from Storage -- this is a strong thing to have in any sort of crafting game. Not sure how games like Nightingale missed this crucial modern feature.
-Unreal Engine updated to version 5.3 from what was originally 4.25 (graphical overhaul which includes Lumen and so on)

[b]Negatives:[/b]
-Not all environments can be climbed (specific to what has leaves on the wall)
-Crafting will be confusing to most players as it seems very convoluted and all over the place.
-The story thus far is lacking
-Limited options for combat / survival
-Rope climbing takes an eternity. Not even I take this long in real life.
-Numerous bugs in many locations, including the fireplace disappearing/despawning randomly while active in the first cabin. (Requires reloading from a save to fix it)
-Drinking water from the Cantine takes 5x longer to refil your thirst over drinking from a water stream / river. (Cantine should be consumed faster in actuality)

The graphics are phenomenal but it really feels like the devs are concentrating more on graphics than gameplay. The UI is clunky and hard to navigate, the gameplay sometimes just instantly  kills you or locks you in a death loop with no instructions or tutorial on how to get out of it, or just breaks entirely to where you are forced to alt+f4 your way out. There were several times in the storyline tutorial where I was simply stuck with no clear instructions on what I was supposed to be doing (It tells you to wave your torch to ward off a wolf, then says don't wave it too much or it'll go out? So don't wave it a lot, but that's what you're supposed to do to get past that stage of the tutorial?) Why does it expect you to spend time reading their tutorial and journal sections, but the game doesn't pause when you're doing so?

There's a lot of things that make no sense that it just expects you to know. Why is my screen always flashing red even at full health, food, and water? Why am I traumatized when nothing has happened to me? Why can't I put snow in a cup or pan and put that on a fire to make water? Why can't I just make an axe? I have all the ingredients, but can only get it through storyline tutorial?

Why is there a leader board and competitive events for "longest survived time" gameplay, when the survival gameplay itself clearly isn't finished?

My biggest critique of the game so far, coming from a mental health standpoint: The game gives a big warning that it deals with mental health issues and treats them respectfully at the beginning... then absolutely [i]does not.[/i] As someone who has experienced visual and auditory hallucinations all their life, that's simply just not how they work. You would not get them that quickly in [i]any[/i] situation unless something else was causing them, such as severe brain trauma (that amount of trauma would quickly have you in a coma within an hour or two max) or hallucinogenic substances of some kind. The deer would not randomly walk out of the bushes, it would have moved when you first encountered the body. Things like that. This is yet another game that relies on 'hallucinations' for a 'sanity system' then has done no research on how visual hallucinations actually manifest.

So yes, while this game has great [i[bones[/i], it still needs a [i]lot[/i] of work before I would recommend it.

The game is engaging. And, it is challenging. It is not supposed to be the Long Dark, or Green Hell, or any other survival type game. And, it very much isn’t. I am very glad for that. It’s also pretty clear they got a lot of influence from them.

But, it has problems.

The Steam blurb says this the “ultimate survival experience,” with a “unique sanity system.” And, I did not really find that to be true about this game. The UI is fairly standard. The injuries and treatments are pretty standard. Injuries and illnesses affect your sanity. Again, pretty standard. 

There is a sanity component. But, it isn’t explained. It’s just kind of sprung on you in pieces. So, you don’t really know how it works or what to do about it.

Survival Mode:
I played about 15 hours of survival mode. And, in Survival Mode, there are 4 scenario options you can choose from, but the game doesn’t explain them well.

The map is small. I believe it is smaller than any zone in The Long Dark. But, wherever you start, sections of it are blocked off to you unless/until you get higher level tools. (I think. Again, not explained.)
I play with a controller due to a nerve issue in my left arm. And, with the controller plugged in, it still shows the mouse on the screen. Unless you move the mouse. Then it disappears. Once it disappears, if you ever need to use it, the mouse never appears on the screen. And, there are situations where you still need the mouse.

The control functions are inconsistnt. It is normal to hit the “use” button (could be either A or X) before the game does whatever it is supposed to do. Many times when trying to use an inventory item, nothing happens. Many other functions often require you to hit the action button twice for anything to happen.
About 5 or 6 hours in, the inventory item display quit working. So, I could not tell what an item is or does. There is a button you can hit that is supposed to enable that…but it doesn’t. Or, if it does, it only displays for some items not all.

There are challenges available in the game. The game tells you when they become available. But, when you go to accept one, it says you can only have one challenge open at a time…even if one is not listed as active. Which can also happen if nothing is listed in the quests, side quests, or challenges.

Story Mode
I am now playing Story Mode (about 6 hours in). The control issues and functionality problems are there, too. Story mode is very linear and scripted. While you can wander around and see what’s what, it is not open world. If you get out of sync with the progression, it is very difficult to get back to the right place and pick it back up again.

Final thoughts:
I like the game. It has a lot going for it. AND! When I posted those problems (and a few others) in their Discord, I got a relatively quick response. Some of it they already knew about, some they didn’t. But, they quickly indicated they are working on them. Which is fantastic.

So, I do recommend this game…with a LOT of caveats. Even so, because of Steam’s recommendation system, my recommendation is to avoid this one. Or, if you do decide to get it, at least buy it at a STEEP discount if you can. In it’s current Early Access state, it is heavily over priced.

[h1] Bloody, Intense... and Borderline Unplayable [/h1] 

[b] Four-Minute Video Review: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f2Pi8KS9tGQ&ab_channel=MEGAthemicro [/b]  

The aptly named “Winter Survival” is a (to probably nobody’s surprise) survival crafting title set in a snow-covered, wolf-infested wasteland that features a psychological horror twist with both narrative and gameplay implications. But the immersion doesn’t stop there! No, for while your player character slowly loses his mind due to the compounded trauma associated with hiding from hungry Grizzly Bears, fighting off relentless wolfpacks, and battling the omnipresent forces of huger and hypothermia, so too will you lose your mind thanks to the litany of game-breaking bugs that Winter Survival has yet to iron out in advance of its Early Access release. 

[b] THE BAD [/b] 

I knew both my player and I were in grave danger within minutes of booting up the prologue, when a cardboard NPC—one of several from this forsaken snow trip—entered a cave, took a squat, and went fully catatonic, refusing to say anything thus killing the quest’s ability to advance. “No problem,” I said, “Let’s reload and try again.” Only this time, replace the broken NPC with an improperly spawned Brown bear, who really, really, didn’t appreciate me trying to play a video game in his cave. While I was, after a third restart, finally able to progress past this cave of doom, I would sadly go on to have a strange gameplay glitch or all-out crash every 45 minutes or so over the course of my eight brutal hours with Winter Survival. 

[b] THE EVEN WORSE [/b] 

But believe it or not, things get worse. Because this game is intentionally punishing in [i] all [/i] aspects: not just in its survival mechanics, but also in its unwillingness to let you save. I could grit my teeth and bear a crash every hour if (A) the gameplay was compelling, and (B) the game included an auto-save feature that could insulate you from those backbreaker bugs that send you back 20, 30, 40, 50(!) minutes in time each time. No such luck here, unfortunately, as Winter Survival only lets you save when you return to your small, half-frozen bed.  

Now, on paper, this design decision makes perfect sense: increase the tension for every extra minute you spend scavenging for supplies away from home, because at any moment a stray wolf you failed to pick up with your Survival Instincts (a scan that reveals items, prey, and predators) could sucker-punch your throat with its two-and-a-half-inch teeth. However, in reality—a reality that often resets itself not via gameplay but game-breaking bugs—Winter Survival becomes a frustrating, unfun, and borderline unplayable mess that earns the channel’s second-ever “1” for Playability, and that's before accounting for how tedious it is to interact with and gather resources in this game. 

Much like I debated stopping my Winter Survival playthrough after the third crash, I debated stopping this review here... because what am I going to say at this point that would make you even consider the game? 

[b] THE GOOD [/b] 

Well, believe it or not, Winter Survival does have some good ideas that make me oh so cautiously optimistic that it might turn things around by 1.0. First, the game ties its skill tree (AKA the “Adaptation system”) to your level of trauma. If you spend too much time hungry, thirsty, in the dark, or running from wolves, your brain will figuratively rot—reach 100% trauma and you’ll not only gain a permanent debuff, like your vision going occasionally blurry when you activate your Survivial Instincts scan, but you’ll also lose an adaptation that you can then regain after completing a challenge, like staying warm for more than half the day. To me, these are fun little twists on the typically stale and static skill tree featured in other genre peers.  

Second, Winter Survival’s open world level design encourages bold exploration. There are some eye-popping points of interest scattered about the map that combine with your increasingly frequent hallucinations to create a trippy, immersive experience.  

And, finally, third, the game features a simple yet effective voice-acted story mode that does a nice job of tying each gameplay mechanic into the narrative.  

[b] CONCLUSION [/b] 

Add in some occasionally excellent visuals and solid, unsettling ambient sound design, and it’s not impossible to envision Winter Survival becoming a worthwhile experience. For anyone feeling adventurous (and masochistic!), I have two free keys I’ll be giving away to random commenters, so let me know if you’d be interested in playtesting this game for the devs, because that’s what Early Access is, right?
